Source note: Uploaded AV public-record review and current public listing/assessment sources. The original working review already identified 1011 as ~11,633 sf, a 1911 1,320-sf home, and R-12. Public AVMs vary materially and should not be substituted for a broker price opinion or appraisal.

3. The one-foot discovery — the key record reconstruction

The most important later finding is that the owner’s memory of a “1 ft” issue on the south side aligns with the public record. The current legal description published for 1007 N B Street includes “S 1 Ft Of Lt 2, Lt 3, N2 Of Lt 4 Block 3.” Separately, the Kootenai County section-map revision notes state that on 23 February 2012 a portion of C-3510-003-001-A — the 1011 parcel — was combined with 003-A, the parcel identifier used for 1007.

High-confidence reconstruction, not a survey The Forest Heights block map repeatedly uses an original ~50-foot lot module and ~117.5-foot depth. If 1007 consists of 1 foot of Lot 2 + 50 feet of Lot 3 + 25 feet (north half) of Lot 4, its reconstructed frontage is ~76 feet. 76 × 117.5 = 8,930 sf, which matches the 8,930-sf public-record lot size reported for 1007. That leaves a plausible ~49 feet of Lot 2 with 1011, plus the original 50-foot Lot 1: approximately 99 feet of frontage. 99 × 117.5 = 11,632.5 sf, essentially matching the reported 11,633 sf at 1011. This is unusually coherent evidence, but it is still not survey-grade.

4. R-12 rules that matter to this decision

Rule Current standard Why it matters
Detached SFR lot area 5,500 sf per detached single-family lot Two conventional SFR lots need at least 11,000 sf total.
Other residential density 3,500 sf per unit except detached SFR A duplex/two-unit path is easier by area than a two-lot detached-SFR split.
Buildable-lot frontage 50 ft on a public street unless an alternative is approved through normal subdivision procedure or lot is nonconforming The apparent 99-ft condition is the subdivision bottleneck.
Frontage definition Front lot line and its length; usually the side nearest/abutting the street Supports testing a front-only boundary adjustment.
R-12 yards 20 ft front; 5 ft interior side; one 10-ft side if no alley/legal rear access; 25 ft rear Survey must prove the existing house and 1007 structures remain lawful after any line movement.
Subdivision access Each lot needs public-street frontage sufficient for legal access or zoning minimum, whichever is greater A future short plat still needs engineering/planning review.
Short vs formal plat Four or fewer lots/no new ROW is a short plat; a lot below Title 17 frontage pushes the division into formal-plat definition Recovering 100 ft could avoid the below-frontage trigger.
Boundary-line adjustment One common line; no new lots; max two deflection points; resulting lots must comply; Idaho surveyor; City approval; warranty deed recorded The proposed 30-ft jog is structurally compatible with the BLA code, subject to City approval.

5. Proposed owner-side solution: front 30-foot boundary gift

The recommended concept is deliberately smaller than the original full-depth one-foot reacquisition. The line would move approximately 1.00 foot south at the B Street/right-of-way frontage, continue west for approximately 30 feet, then return north approximately 1.00 foot to the existing common boundary before the area where the 1007 garage may be at or near its existing setback. The remaining western common boundary stays unchanged.

User-supplied GIS/aerial annotation. Blue marks the proposed front-only adjustment; yellow identifies the 1007 garage concern. Parcel overlays are not a boundary survey.

AeroVista concept schematic. The one-foot offset is exaggerated for visibility. Final line and legal description must come from an Idaho licensed surveyor.

6. Why the 30-foot version is better than a full-depth strip

It targets the actual bottleneck: B Street frontage.

It transfers only about 30 square feet instead of roughly 117.5 square feet.

It keeps the existing common line in place near the 1007 garage, reducing the risk of making a tight garage setback worse.

It can be drawn with two deflection points, which is the maximum allowed by the City BLA approval rule.

It leaves 1007 with roughly 75 feet of street frontage if the 76-foot reconstruction is correct — still well above the normal 50-foot R-12 requirement.

It does not appear to take away a conventional two-lot split from 1007; ~75–76 feet is already less than the 100 feet normally needed for two 50-foot-frontage lots.

It preserves the neighbor relationship because the physical impact is tiny and can be conditioned on causing no new nonconformity.

7. Conceptual subdivision math after the gift

If the survey confirms the working geometry of approximately 99 ft × 117.5 ft and the gift widens only the first 30 feet to 100 feet, the conceptual total area becomes about 11,662.5 sf. A future line 50 feet from the north boundary could produce the following rough geometry:

Conceptual future lot Approx. frontage Approx. area R-12 area test
North lot 50 ft 5,875 sf Pass by ~375 sf
South lot 50 ft at B Street; ~49 ft wide behind the 30-ft front segment 5,787.5 sf Pass by ~287.5 sf
Critical City question The area math works, but the southern future lot would narrow behind the 30-foot frontage segment. Title 17 states a 50-foot frontage requirement; it does not expressly say the lot must remain 50 feet wide for its full depth. That does not equal approval. Before accepting the gift as the solution, obtain written Planning/Engineering confirmation that this irregular geometry is acceptable for a future two-lot subdivision and that no other dimensional/design standard defeats it.

8. Existing structures: 1011 house and 1007 garage

The current GIS/aerial imagery is useful for screening but not for setback determinations. The 1007 garage appears close to the common line. The City measures setbacks to the wall of a structure, not simply the roof edge. The front-30-ft concept is specifically designed to return to the existing line before the garage and therefore should not worsen the garage-side line — but only an improvement/boundary survey can prove this.

Survey the shortest perpendicular distance from every 1007 structure wall to both the current and proposed boundary.

Survey the exact 1011 house footprint and test the potential future 50/50 frontage split line against the house and required side yard.

Confirm whether either property has an alley or other legal rear access because that changes the 10-foot-side-yard rule.

Locate fences, driveways, sewer/water service, utility lines, recorded easements, and any encroachments before City submission.

Source note: The City BLA application expressly requires dimensions to existing/proposed boundaries, structures, sewer/water service, street frontage and access. The uploaded City setback sheet likewise shows 20-ft front, 5-ft interior side, one 10-ft side without alley/rear access, and 25-ft rear standards as the working residential framework.

9. Other development paths remain valuable

Subdivision is the highest-leverage quick-exit story only if it can be proven cheaply. It is not the only development right. Current CDA code allows up to two detached dwelling units on a qualifying lot when minimum lot size is met; R-12 also supports duplex housing. The current ADU code allows an ADU up to 800 sf (and up to 75% of the primary dwelling), requires one additional parking space, and does not allow the ADU to be separately subdivided under the current ADU rule.

Path Capital burden Current AV view
Front-30-ft BLA + prove two-lot split Low/moderate Best owner-side value unlock if City confirms geometry.
Sell as one R-12 parcel with two-dwelling potential Low Strong fallback if split cannot be proven quickly.
Retain house + second detached dwelling High Potentially strong long-term development, but wrong fit for a cash-constrained quick exit.
Retain house + ADU Moderate Lower-risk hold strategy; subordinate unit and current 800-sf cap reduce exit flexibility.
Demolish/rebuild duplex High Entitlement by area is attractive, but destroys existing asset and triggers demolition review because the 1911 structure predates 1960.

10. Demolition is not the near-term recommendation

Coeur d’Alene currently subjects structures originally constructed before 1960 to Historic Preservation Commission demolition review before a demolition permit can be issued. The code makes clear that the review process does not permanently deny an owner the right to demolish, but it adds process, documentation, and timing. With a 1911 house and a financially constrained owner, demolition should remain a developer/buyer decision unless there is a compelling separate reason to pursue it.

11. Value impact — use as strategy, not an appraisal

The current automated market signals for 1011 are broad: roughly $554,500 (Redfin estimate), $584,700 (Realtor estimate), and $631,600 (Zillow Zestimate) in the sources reviewed. Those are not appraisals. The relevant market question is how much certainty around a second legal lot changes a buyer’s willingness to pay.

Milestone Owner-side planning range for incremental value How to use it
Gift/BLA concept only Do not price a premium yet Useful story, not entitlement.
Survey + title + City written feasibility ~$75k–$150k internal AV scenario Potentially marketable entitlement premium; get broker/BPO validation.
Preliminary two-lot approval ~$100k–$200k internal AV scenario Stronger developer certainty; balance premium against time/cost.
Two recorded, independently transferable lots ~$150k–$250k+ internal AV scenario Highest certainty, but not necessarily best return for a broke owner if process becomes expensive.

A current downtown R-12 “ready to build” 4,792-sf lot at 1210 N 10th St has been marketed around $315,000. Another 4,792-sf Sanders Beach lot at 310 S 16th St has been marketed around $399,900, illustrating that small infill lot asking prices vary widely by micro-location and readiness. Those listings support the idea that an independently buildable downtown lot can carry material value, but they do not establish what a future 1011-created lot would sell for.

Owner-side pricing rule Do not sell the owner’s urgency. Sell certainty. The owner’s best low-cash move is to convert “maybe a double lot” into a documented survey/title/City package and then require a buyer to pay for the upside.

12. Gift-first negotiation strategy with 1007

Because the owners are reportedly friends, the opening should be simple, accurate, and low-pressure. The request is for a gift of only the front portion of the historical one-foot strip, subject to survey and City approval and designed to return to the current line before the garage. The owner should not begin by offering money.

Suggested first conversation “We found an old county record showing a one-foot piece from 1011 was combined with your parcel years ago. We’re checking whether correcting only the front ~30 feet would help clean up our frontage. Would you be open to gifting that tiny front piece back if a survey and the City confirm it doesn’t create any problem for your property? We’d structure it so the line goes back to where it is now before your garage. No pressure — if the survey shows it hurts your property, we stop.”

Do not characterize the gift as “tax free.” 1007 should obtain its own tax advice.

Do not promise that 1007 loses no value; say the transaction is conditioned on survey/City review showing no new nonconformity and let 1007 obtain independent advice.

Do not reveal a six-figure internal value estimate unless it becomes strategically necessary and the owner approves.

If 1007 declines a gift, stop and return to the 1011 owner for authority before introducing money. No pre-authorized cash ladder is included in this report.

If 1007 agrees in principle, move immediately to a short written gift proposal and survey-access consent so neither side relies on memory.

13. Gift tax / basis / lender issues

A real-property gift can have federal gift-tax reporting and basis consequences. The 2026 annual gift-tax exclusion is $19,000 per donee. A gift over the annual exclusion can require Form 709 reporting even when no immediate gift tax is owed because of the donor’s lifetime exclusion. Property received by gift generally carries the donor’s adjusted basis for gain purposes, subject to special rules. Because the strip may have assemblage or “plottage” value to 1011 beyond its raw square footage, neither side should guess at fair market value. 1007 should consult its own CPA/attorney. The 1011 owner should retain the deed, survey, and any value allocation for basis records.

If 1007 is mortgaged, the transferred area may be part of the lender’s collateral. A title company should determine whether a partial release/reconveyance or lender consent is required before recording. The gift agreement should be expressly contingent on obtaining any required lender consent without liability to the 1011 owner.

14. Exact transaction path for the 30-foot gift

1. Friend-first verbal request: ask whether 1007 is willing in principle to gift the approximately 1 ft × 30 ft front area, with the line returning before the garage.

2. Sign the short Neighbor Gift Proposal / Letter of Intent and Survey Access Consent from the companion transaction package.

3. Order a boundary + improvement survey of both common-line areas. Tell the surveyor the specific objective: determine exact B Street frontage and design a BLA with no more than two deflection points that adds approximately one foot of frontage to 1011 for roughly the first 30 feet of depth.

4. Order current title reports for both parcels. Confirm ownership, legal creation, easements, liens, deeds of trust, and any lender consent/partial release requirement.

5. Have the surveyor prepare a preliminary Record of Survey and metes-and-bounds legal description of the transferred area. The concept, not the user’s sketch, becomes Exhibit A.

6. Before incurring major expense, submit the concept to CDA Planning/Engineering and ask for written confirmation on the two critical points: adjusted 1011 frontage and future two-lot acceptability of the 50-ft-frontage/49-ft-interior-width southern lot geometry.

7. If the City response is favorable, execute the Conditional Boundary Line Adjustment & Gift Agreement and submit the City BLA application. Current City-wide fee schedule lists the Engineering BLA fee at $750.

8. Satisfy City comments. The City code requires an Idaho licensed surveyor, no more than two deflection points, compliant resulting lots, no impaired easements/access, and sewer/water service.

9. After approval and any lender release, 1007 signs the Gift Warranty Deed containing the surveyor’s metes-and-bounds Exhibit A. The City code specifically requires a warranty deed for the transferred area and requires its recording instrument number to be referenced on the Record of Survey.

10. Record the deed and approved Record of Survey with Kootenai County in the sequence directed by the City/title company. County recording requirements include an original/completed document, grantor signature, notarization, and legal description or related instrument reference.

11. Obtain updated assessor/GIS records and a final title update showing the boundary adjustment.

12. Immediately package the new evidence for sale. Only pursue the $350 preliminary-plat preapplication meeting and $1,000 preliminary short-subdivision application if the expected sale premium exceeds the added delay/cost.

15. Owner-side 14-day sprint

When Action Stop/continue rule
Day 0–1 Friend conversation + gift proposal No cash offer. If “no,” stop and report back to owner.
Day 1–3 Get 2–3 survey quotes; order title reports Choose smallest scope that still proves frontage, structures, easements, and BLA geometry.
Day 3–10 Field survey + preliminary BLA exhibit Stop if exact geometry cannot produce a defensible ≥100.00-ft frontage or causes new nonconformity.
Day 7–12 City mini/preapplication review / written question Continue only if City treats front-only jog as viable and future two-lot geometry is acceptable or has a clear alternative.
Day 10–14 Sign binding gift agreement and file BLA Only after title/lender path is known and owner approves budget.
Immediately after proof Prepare sale package/BPO outreach Monetize certainty; avoid construction unless sale market proves entitlement premium is insufficient.

16. Hard decision gates

Gate Green Red / fallback
Exact 1011 frontage Surveyed adjusted frontage ≥100.00 ft as recognized by City If still <100 ft, ask about frontage alternative; otherwise sell as one two-dwelling R-12 parcel.
1007 structures No new nonconformity/encroachment from proposed 30-ft BLA Redraw shorter/diagonal return or abandon gift.
1011 existing house Future split line + setbacks can coexist with house, or buyer accepts demolition/rebuild path If house blocks split and demolition economics fail, market two-dwelling single-parcel use instead.
City interpretation Written confirmation that proposed geometry can support short-plat path Do not market “two legal lots” without this.
Title/lender Clear conveyance path and any partial release obtainable Do not record around a lender or easement problem.
Owner cash Due-diligence spend stays within owner-approved cap Stop at proof-of-feasibility and sell the opportunity rather than financing entitlement completion.

17. Surveyor instruction — copy/paste scope

Establish the exact B Street frontage and full boundary of APN C3510003001A (1011 N B St) and the shared north boundary of APN C3510003003A (1007 N B St). Locate all structures and improvements within at least 15 feet of the common line, including wall faces, eaves, garage, fences, driveways, utilities, and visible service lines. Prepare a boundary-line-adjustment alternate that moves the common boundary approximately 1.00 foot south at the B Street frontage, continues west approximately 30.00 feet, then returns north to the existing common boundary before the 1007 garage/setback area, using no more than two deflection points. Show existing and proposed frontage, parcel areas, structure setbacks, sewer/water service, access, easements, and the conceptual future division of 1011 into two lots with 50-foot frontage each. Prepare metes-and-bounds descriptions suitable for City BLA and warranty deed exhibits. Do not treat GIS parcel lines as survey control.

18. Questions to put to CDA in writing

1. If the BLA gives 1011 a surveyed 100.00-foot B Street front lot line for the first ~30 feet and the south boundary then jogs one foot north, does the City recognize 100.00 feet of frontage for R-12 §17.05.230(B)?

2. Can 1011 then be divided into two R-12 detached-SFR lots with 50 feet of street frontage each where one resulting lot narrows to roughly 49 feet behind the front ~30 feet, provided each lot exceeds 5,500 sf and all setbacks/access standards are satisfied?

3. Would that division be processed as a preliminary short subdivision rather than a formal plat?

4. Does the existing 1011 house appear capable of remaining on one resulting lot if the licensed survey confirms the required side setback?

5. Does any existing alley, rear legal access, utility condition, right-of-way dedication, or frontage improvement requirement affect this block?

6. What exact BLA submission, deed-recording sequence, and lender-release documentation does Engineering want for this two-deflection-point line?

19. Data quality and unresolved items

Exact legal descriptions for 1011 and the proposed gift area are not yet in hand from a surveyor/title report.

GIS/aerial parcel lines are reference graphics only and cannot establish a setback or ownership boundary.

The ~99 × 117.5-ft reconstruction is high-confidence analytical work, not a boundary survey.

The 1007 public listing reports 8,930 sf in public records, while some listing summaries show 8,712 sf; use the title/survey acreage, not listing metadata.

AVMs disagree materially on 1011 value. Use a current local broker price opinion or appraisal before setting an asking price.

Permit history, exact utility laterals/capacity, and authoritative zoning verification remain open diligence items.

A previously archived “Midtown” investor package containing 93-ft frontage/foreclosure facts was not used because those facts do not match the 1011 property record and appear to relate to another deal.

20. Final AV recommendation

GO — with a disciplined stop rule Ask for the gift first. Prove the front 30-foot BLA with survey/title/City confirmation. If that proof is clean, record the BLA if the owner-approved cost is modest, then sell the newly documented subdivision upside. Do not spend the broke owner’s money on a build, demolition, or polished architecture. If the BLA does not produce a defensible future two-lot path, pivot immediately and market 1011 on its existing R-12 two-dwelling potential instead of chasing an expensive exception.
